interest: For historians, this file provides an invaluable, real-time diplomatic lens into Japan’s rapid transition from parliamentary governance to entrenched military domination and wartime mobilization between 1936 and 1938. Ambassador Grew's granular monthly reports uniquely capture the domestic trials, purges, and cabinet collapses following the February 26 Incident alongside first-hand diplomatic assessments of critical international turning points, including the signing of the Anti-Comintern Pact and the outbreak of the war in China. Additionally, it offers exceptional contemporary documentation of crisis diplomacy and Western responses to early wartime atrocities, urban aerial bombardments, and direct attacks on foreign assets, such as the U.S.S. Panay and British gunboats on the Yangtze River.
overview: This file comprises regular monthly political, diplomatic, and economic reports alongside accompanying transmittal despatches and communication schedules sent by the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo—primarily under Ambassador Joseph C. Grew—to the Department of State between March 1936 and January 1938. Spanning the immediate aftermath of the February 26 Incident through the early months of the second Sino-Japanese War, the collection provides comprehensive contemporary documentation of Japan's domestic political crises, military ascendance, and economic mobilization across the successive Okada, Hirota, Hayashi, and Konoe Cabinets. Internationally, the records chronicle escalating armed confrontations in North China leading to all-out war after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, the conclusion of the Anti-Comintern Pact with Germany and Italy, border clashes with the Soviet Union, and mounting diplomatic flashpoints with Western powers, culminating in the capture of Nanking and the international crisis over the sinking of the U.S.S. Panay.
